title: Google Suncatcher Satellite Launches With Gemma 4 in Orbit
summary: Google's first space data center satellite is online, running Gemma 4 inference workloads in orbit. The TPU-equipped spacecraft paves the way for 2027
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Google Suncatcher's prototype orbital data center went live this week, successfully running Gemma 4 inference on a space-based TPU after launching earlier in October 2026.
- The satellite generates 1 kW of power and operates in 20-minute bursts, testing how radiation and thermal stress affect chip performance during real orbital conditions.
- Two additional satellites with higher power and inter-satellite optical links will launch in 2027 as Google builds toward economical space inference infrastructure for the 2030s.


Google Suncatcher's first orbital data center satellite is now operational and running inference workloads in space. The spacecraft, equipped with a single Google Tensor Processing Unit and Google DeepMind's Gemma 4 model, completed commissioning this week and responded to its first prompt from ground engineers with a haiku about starlight and data streams. The milestone marks a critical step toward networks of close-flying satellites performing large-scale AI inference beyond Earth's atmosphere.


## Release Date and Operational Status


Officially launched on October 30, 2026, the Suncatcher prototype rode to orbit aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket alongside more than 100 other spacecraft earlier this month. After three weeks of commissioning tests validating the satellite's subsystems, engineers activated the TPU and sent their first inference request. The spacecraft is operating nominally according to a Google spokesperson, with the model successfully generating poetry and reporting orbital condition data back to ground control.


## Power Constraints and Technical Challenges


The satellite generates up to 1 kilowatt of electricity, but the power-hungry TPU can only operate for approximately 20 minutes at a time. This limitation complicates space-to-ground communications and constrains the duration of inference sessions. The short operational windows require precise coordination between satellite passes and ground station availability, adding complexity to what is already a challenging technical endeavor in the space environment.


## Radiation Testing and Chip Performance


The ongoing test campaign focuses on how Google's TPUs perform under thermal stress and exposure to space radiation. While Google extensively tested its chips in particle accelerators on Earth, real orbital conditions present different challenges. Radiation can cause bit flips in computer memory, corrupting data without triggering standard monitoring tools. Ground-based testing suggested minimal impact on inference workloads compared to model training, but the team will now validate those predictions in actual space operations rather than simulations.


## 2027 Expansion and Starcloud Vision


If the current TPU proves capable during its orbital trial, Google plans to launch two additional satellites in 2027. Those next-generation spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links, a capability central to Google's Starcloud project vision. Unlike competitors such as SpaceX and Cowboy Space, which plan individual satellite inference loads, Google is designing high-speed links between satellites to enable coherent distributed workloads across orbital constellations.


## Long-Term Economics and Market Context


Suncatcher represents a classic moonshot bet on infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Both Google and SpaceX require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket, to achieve full and rapid reusability before orbital data centers become financially viable. A peer-reviewed analysis published in October 2026 estimates SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the learning-driven cost reductions seen with earlier vehicles. The timeline faces pressure from Alphabet's near-term AI challenges, including this week's stock decline after reports that AI integration into search businesses is hurting ad revenue growth.


## What This Means


Google Suncatcher's successful activation validates the technical feasibility of space-based AI inference, even as power and radiation constraints remain significant hurdles. The 2027 expansion with inter-satellite links will determine whether distributed orbital workloads can operate as a coherent system. For organizations planning long-term AI infrastructure strategies, Suncatcher offers a glimpse of how inference might migrate beyond terrestrial data centers, though economic viability depends on breakthroughs in launch costs and satellite power generation over the next decade.
